chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
title: First bands and the first job at the Gypsy Tea Room
summary: He names bands he played in and recalls his first job, six months after getting the horn, where older players made him put the music away.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah. Can you tell us anything about the first bands you ever played in? Did you ever play with anybody with your guitar before you took up sax? Did you ever hit bands or anything else?

Well, I played in quite a number of bands around, but I played like the Tuxedo band. I played with them. Like I tell you, I played with the Yara band. I played with the Tarny Tribe band. It was by Professor Pritchett. He had a band around in the District 4th of War, about 39 or 40. What was your very first job?
Do you remember what that was?

The first job I played, to tell you the positive, the truth, was about six months after I got the horn. I played a job. Oh, yeah. And the first job I played was down in the Gypsy Tea Room. Oh, yeah. Down on Royal Street. They had a Gypsy Tea Room was down there. And the people was head that day, they lived somewhere down in the Chalmette, down there by the Shipyard. Right? I forget their name. Then after that, well, I played for the fraternity houses, the carnival time come, you know. But that was the first job I played on. But then the fellas began to tell me, because I had the music up, and they would tell me about the Green Book. See, well, they didn't want you to put up no music. They said, well, get in the Green Book. So they want you to play without the music. So, well, constantly, well, I just come, and I would have music up, and the older fellas, they would take the music down, and make me put it in my case. So that made me have to concentrate more on my music. But then when I come to find out later years, it was better for me to do it that way. Well, I hadn't learned nothing about theory until later on me. Well, in theory, well, I liked the difference between a tone and a note. Well, they tell you that a note is seen, and a tone is heard. So on the other hand, if you can see a note and don't know it when you hear it, well, it's still as bad as not seeing it and don't know it when you make it. So on the other hand, well, the older fellas, they had a good theory on putting your music on the side and using the ear. So now, if I'm not anything I play now, I go and put the music on the side and memorize it, you see, and so forth like that, and I don't have my trouble.
